messages.author: 13d0e40ead8b0219
messages.subject: Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
parts:
Hi Karl,

I'm trying to identify sibs in our population of DO mice. My idea is to create a kinship matrix, scale it using scale_kinship(), then identifying pairs with a scaled kinship of ~0.5

Does that make sense? Am I understanding the scaled kinship values correctly, where a kinship of ~0.5 signifies siblings?

Thanks,
Basel Al-Barghouthi

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
parts:
I would ignore the scale_kinship() function. I think the unscaled kinship, straight from calc_kinship(), should be sufficient for your purposes.

But note that the kinship coefficient should be 1/4 for non-inbred siblings and 1/2 for non-inbred individual-to-self. (See for example https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coefficient_of_relationship).

DO siblings should be a bit more closely related than siblings, because their parents will be somewhat related. And so you should expect to see kinship coefficients > 0.5 along the diagonal and > 0.25 for sibs.

You could try using the simcross package to simulate DO mice and look at their kinship matrix.
Here's an example: https://gist.github.com/kbroman/ee0465bab33c0f7425524d0b003d0165

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
parts:
I haven't studied the estimated kinship coefficients for DO mice, and the data I have are not supposed to contain any siblings.
I do see kinship coefficients in the 0.3-0.4 range. I've presumed that these were like first cousins. For mice in different generations, there could be some aunt-niece type relationships. And since the DO mice are being bred with a finite population size, we have both inbreeding and multiple lines of relationship that will be increasing the kinship coefficients.

There's also just a lot of sampling variation in these sorts of realized kinship coefficients. The proportion of the genome shared by a particular relative pair could be 0.25 on average but will vary a great deal around that.

karl

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
parts:
Looking more closely at the kinship matrix for a DO-related collaboration of mine, it seems like the first batch of 100 mice we got include a bunch of siblings, with kinship coefficients in the 0.3-0.4 range. The other 470 mice in the study don't show any kinship coefficients that big.

Here's an image of the kinship matrix with black = large.



Note all the speckles.

Here's what I get if I use hclust to reorder the mice, something like this:

  h <- hclust(as.dist(-k))
  image(k[h$order, h$order], col=rev(gray((0:256)/256)))



My guess is that those blocks of similar mice are the sibships.

karl

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
parts: Thanks Karl, that's very helpful. Can you please explain how kinship is calculated in the DO using allele probs? I saw the formula in the functions documentation, but I couldn't quite understand it.

messages.author: 96353e7106735838
messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl2-disc] Identifying siblings with kinship matrix
parts:
The allele dosages/probabilities for each individual is a matrix, say markers x alleles. We take two such matrices and multiply them element-wise and then add them up. And that's our estimate of the kinship coefficient.

karl
